newsitem.title: USA: Whitewater lawyer criticized for arguing other case.
newsitem.headline: Whitewater lawyer criticized for arguing other case.

text.p: A Democratic congressman Tuesday criticised independent counsel Kenneth Starr for taking time off from the Whitewater investigation to argue before the Supreme Court on behalf of a military contractor.

Representative Marty Meehan from Massachusetts renewed his criticism of Starr for representing private clients from his private law firm while remaining in charge of the Whitewater investigation involving President Clinton and his wife.

Starr on Friday said he would stay on until the investigation has been "substantially completed," putting on hold his plans to leave for a new career at Pepperdine University and admitting he had made a big mistake.

"After last week's flip-flop, one would think that Starr would do everything in his power to demonstrate his commitment to the Whitewater investigation," said Meehan, a House Judiciary Committee member.
"Now we find him arguing before the Supreme Court on an unrelated matter. Starr just doesn't get it," he said.

Starr argued before the high court for Hughes Aircraft Company over a whistleblower lawsuit by one of its former employees seeking $150 million in damages for alleged mischarged costs under a Pentagon aircraft contract.

"Starr should be working full-time to bring the Whitewater case to a conclusion rather than moonlighting on behalf of private clients. Hughes may be paying for Starr's work today, but it's the taxpayer who foots the bill for the interminable Whitewater investigation," Meehan said in a statement.

Starr for 2-1/2 years has been probing the Whitewater land deal involving the Clintons when the president was governor of Arkansas and failure of an Arkansas savings and loan institution run by James McDougal, their partner in the deal.
The investigation has been expanded to include a number of White House controversies, including the firing of the travel office staff and the obtaining of FBI personal files.
After the arguments, Starr was unavailable for comment. Chris Landau, who works at Starr's private law firm, told reporters that "Hughes has taken a position" of not discussing a pending case.
He said Starr had engaged in a "thorough job" to get ready and took part in practice arguments last week, but he refused to discuss in detail how much time Starr spent on "internal preparations."

Meehan previously criticised Starr for representing the Brown & Williamson Tobacco Co. at the same time as the Justice Department was investigating the tobacco industry. He said it raised questions, especially since Clinton has taken strong anti-tobacco positions.
